pos: n. (cathedral city of the English west country; see of John Hooper, who was burnt in it in 1555)
etymology: From Old English Glēawanceaster, the Roman fort at Glevum; ceaster, a walled town.
biblical_def: Gloucester was John Hooper's diocese and his place of execution. Made bishop in 1551 after a long dispute in which he refused to be consecrated in the traditional vestments, holding that they were not indifferent but a remnant of a false priesthood, he governed Gloucester and Worcester together with a severity toward idle and ignorant clergy that made him enemies and a care for the poor that made him loved. Under Mary he was deprived, imprisoned for eighteen months, condemned, and sent down to his own cathedral city to be burnt on 9 February 1555 in front of the people he had taught. The fire was badly made of green wood and he was nearly three-quarters of an hour dying. The dictionary records Gloucester because the three in the furnace said what Hooper said, and said it before they knew the outcome: “But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods” (Dan 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a furnace as an enclosed fireplace for melting ores, and in Scripture a place of trial; to try as to prove by a test, to purify; and a vestment as a garment, and particularly a garment of ceremony.
webster_full: FURNACE, n. [L. fornax.] A place where a vehement fire is maintained, for melting ores or other substances; in Scripture, a place or state of severe trial.
TRY, v.t. To examine; to prove by a test; to purify; to refine, as metals by fire.
VESTMENT, n. [L. vestimentum.] A garment; some part of clothing or dress; particularly, a garment worn in ceremony.
KINDLE, v.t. To set on fire; to cause to burn with flame; to light.
scriptures: Dan 3:17
If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
Isa 43:2

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: John Hooper's see; he refused the traditional vestments at his consecration and was burnt in his own cathedral city in February 1555.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Hooper fought over the vestments was the retention of a priestly dress for a ministry that is not a priesthood. His opponents, Ridley among them, held the garments to be indifferent and the quarrel needless; Hooper held that a garment which signifies a sacrificing priest is not indifferent while anyone still reads it that way. The dictionary judges Hooper right on the principle and grants that he pressed it at a bad moment, and notes that the two men who disagreed about cloth died in the same cause within a year of each other.

The principle to recover is that the faithful do not require a guaranteed deliverance before they refuse. The three Hebrews state their confidence and then set it aside: “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace” (Dan 3:17), and then the words that make the confession unconditional (Dan 3:18). God's promise to His people in fire is presence rather than exemption: “when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned” (Isa 43:2). And Peter names the purpose of the furnace, that the trial of faith, “though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory” (1Pe 1:7).

pos: n. (cathedral city of the English midlands; see of Hugh Latimer, who resigned it in 1539 rather than subscribe the Six Articles)
etymology: From Old English Wigoraceaster, the Roman fort of the Weogoran tribe; ceaster, a walled town.
biblical_def: Worcester was Hugh Latimer's one diocese and he held it four years. Appointed in 1535, he preached and visited vigorously, had the shrine images of his cathedral removed, and pressed his clergy to teach; and in 1539, when Henry VIII's Six Articles reasserted transubstantiation, auricular confession, clerical celibacy and private masses on pain of death, Latimer resigned the bishopric rather than subscribe them. He never held office again, preached before Edward VI the plainest sermons an English king has heard, and was burnt at Oxford with Ridley in October 1555. The dictionary records Worcester because resignation is one of the few instruments a minister has and Latimer used it rather than sign. Ezekiel was sent out under the same terms: “And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear” (Eze 2:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to subscribe as to attest by writing one's name, and to assent; to forbear as to abstain from, to refrain; and plainness as openness, simplicity, freedom from affectation.
webster_full: SUBSCRIBE, v.t. [L. subscribo.] To attest by writing one's name beneath; to assent to, as to a creed or confession.
FORBEAR, v.i. To stop; to cease; to hold from proceeding; to abstain; to refrain.
PLAINNESS, n. Openness; rough sincerity; artlessness; simplicity; freedom from affectation or ornament.
ENTICE, v.t. To incite or instigate by exciting hope or desire; to allure; to attract.
scriptures: Eze 2:7
And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear: for they are most rebellious.
Jer 1:17
Thou therefore gird up thy loins, and arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee: be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them.
And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
corruption_summary: Hugh Latimer's see for four years; he resigned it in 1539 rather than subscribe the Six Articles, and was burnt at Oxford in 1555.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is subscription against conscience, which the Six Articles made a condition of office and which has been made a condition of office many times since in gentler forms. A man who signs what he does not believe in order to keep a pulpit has already lost the pulpit's only value. Latimer's resignation cost him his income, his influence and eventually the opportunity to shape the Henrician church, and it preserved the one thing that made his later preaching weigh.

The principle to recover is that the preacher's commission is to deliver the message regardless of reception, and to deliver it plainly. Jeremiah is told to expect hostile faces and not to be deflected: “be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them” (Jer 1:17). Paul disclaims the arts of persuasion, saying his preaching was “not with enticing words of man's wisdom” (1Co 2:4), and he disclaims the handling of the text for effect, “nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth” (2Co 4:2).

pos: n. (cathedral city of Wiltshire; see of John Jewel, author of the Apology of the Church of England)
etymology: From Old English Searobyrg, an alteration of the Roman Sorviodunum; burh, a fortified place.
biblical_def: Salisbury was John Jewel's see from 1560 until his death in 1571, and from it he wrote the book that gave the English Reformation its public case. Jewel had been a Marian exile at Frankfurt and Strasbourg; recalled under Elizabeth, he published in 1562 the Apologia Ecclesiae Anglicanae, an answer to the Roman charge that the English church was a novelty, arguing from Scripture first and then from the fathers and the councils of the first six centuries that it was Rome which had innovated. It was translated, answered, and defended through a long controversy with Thomas Harding, and was for a century the standard English statement of the case. The dictionary records the see because Jewel's method is the right one. Paul before Felix admits the name his accusers used and then grounds his position in the text they both claimed: “after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers” (Act 24:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an apology as a defence, something written in vindication of what appears to others wrong; heresy as a fundamental error in religion; and to expound as to explain, to lay open the meaning.
webster_full: APOLOGY, n. [Gr.] A defense; an excuse; something said or written in defense or extenuation of what appears to others wrong.
HERESY, n. [Gr. to choose.] A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
EXPOUND, v.t. [L. expono.] To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
NOVELTY, n. Newness; recentness of origin; something new or unusual; an innovation.
scriptures: But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets:
Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great, saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come:

And when they had appointed him a day, there came many to him into his lodging; to whom he expounded and testified the kingdom of God, persuading them concerning Jesus, both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets, from morning till evening.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
corruption_summary: John Jewel's see; his 1562 Apology answered Rome's charge of novelty from Scripture and the first six centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the Roman argument from prescription: that a doctrine held for a thousand years cannot be an innovation, and that whatever is newly stated must be newly invented. Jewel's answer was to show that the practices in dispute were themselves late arrivals, and that the first centuries did not know them. The argument still has to be made, and the English church's own later history shows the opposite danger, an appeal to antiquity so fond that the fathers come to outrank the apostles.

The principle to recover is the order of appeal: Scripture first, the ancient church as a witness to Scripture, and nothing beyond. Paul describes his own ministry as having said nothing new, “saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come” (Act 26:22). At Rome he spent a whole day on the same ground, “persuading them concerning Jesus, both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets, from morning till evening” (Act 28:23). And Christ Himself set the pattern on the Emmaus road: “beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27).

“saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come” (Act 26:22) — a Marian exile recalled under Elizabeth.
“beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27) — the see held from 1560 to 1571.

pos: n. (cathedral city of Norfolk; where Thomas Bilney was burnt in 1531)
etymology: From Old English Northwic, the northern trading settlement; wic, a dwelling or port.
biblical_def: Norwich was the second city of England at the Reformation and the place where Thomas Bilney died. Bilney, a Cambridge fellow known as Little Bilney, had bought a copy of Erasmus's Greek New Testament for its Latin, and reading in it came on one sentence that broke a long search for peace of conscience through fasting, vigils and confession: he said afterwards that it was as if a bone long out of joint had been set. He preached to the eastern counties, recanted under pressure in 1527, repented of the recantation, preached again in Norfolk, and was burnt in the Lollards' Pit outside Norwich in August 1531. The dictionary records the city because the verse that converted him is the one the church exists to say, and because a man who had failed once went back to say it: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (1Ti 1:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conversion as a change from one state to another, and in theology a change of heart from sin to God; acceptation as reception with approbation; and longsuffering as patient endurance under provocation.
webster_full: CONVERSION, n. [L. conversio.] In a theological or moral sense, a change of heart, or dispositions, in which the enmity of the heart to God is subdued, and is succeeded by love and obedience.
ACCEPTATION, n. Kind reception; a receiving with favor or approbation; the meaning or sense in which a word is understood.
LONGSUFFERING, n. Continuance of patience under provocation or injury; patient endurance.
PATTERN, n. An original or model proposed for imitation; the archetype; an exemplar.
scriptures: This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
Howbeit for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe on him to life everlasting.
For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.
Mat 9:13
But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
corruption_summary: Norfolk's cathedral city; Thomas Bilney, converted by one sentence in Erasmus's New Testament, was burnt in the Lollards' Pit in 1531.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Bilney was delivered from is the one his own practices had served: the attempt to quiet a guilty conscience by religious exertion, which Rome systematised in penance, satisfaction and the merit of works, and which answers the symptom and leaves the disease. He had done everything the system prescribed and was no nearer peace. The modern form prescribes self-acceptance instead of satisfaction and reaches the same dead end, because neither addresses the guilt that is actually there.

The principle to recover is that Christ came for sinners as such, and that the chief of them is the pattern rather than the exception. Paul says his own case was arranged for display, that “in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe” (1Ti 1:16). Christ states His errand in one line, “For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luk 19:10), and tells His critics where to look it up: “I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Mat 9:13).

pos: n. (cathedral city of Kent; see of Nicholas Ridley, and before him of John Fisher, who died for the opposite cause)
etymology: From Old English Hrofesceaster, the Roman fort at Durobrivae; ceaster, a walled town.
biblical_def: Rochester is the English see whose two most famous bishops died, twelve years apart, for contrary convictions. John Fisher held it from 1504 and was beheaded in 1535 for refusing the royal supremacy, a Roman churchman of real learning and real courage. Nicholas Ridley was appointed in 1547, moved to London in 1550, and was burnt at Oxford with Latimer in 1555; the doctrine on which he was condemned was the Lord's Supper, and he held that the bread remains bread and that Christ is received by faith, against the transubstantiation Fisher had defended. The dictionary records the see because the question between them is the question, and the words of institution are where it must be settled. Paul reports them as he received them: the Lord “brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a remembrance as the retaining in memory, a memorial; transubstantiation as the change of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ; and a testament as a covenant, and the dispensation of the gospel.
webster_full: REMEMBRANCE, n. The retaining or having in mind the idea of a thing which had been present; also, a memorial; that which serves to keep in mind.
TRANSUBSTANTIATION, n. In the Romish church, the supposed conversion of the bread and wine in the eucharist into the body and blood of Christ.
TESTAMENT, n. [L. testamentum.] A solemn authentic instrument in writing; also, the covenant between God and man, and the dispensation of the gospel.
SUPREMACY, n. State of being supreme or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.
scriptures: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body.
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
corruption_summary: The Kentish see of John Fisher, beheaded in 1535, and of Nicholas Ridley, burnt in 1555 for denying transubstantiation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is transubstantiation, defined at the Fourth Lateran Council and dogmatised at Trent: that the substance of the bread and wine is converted into the body and blood of Christ, the appearances alone remaining, so that the mass is a true propitiatory sacrifice offered by a priest. Rome holds this still. The dictionary names it as error on three grounds: it contradicts the plain sense of the words in which Christ, holding bread, said the words over it; it makes a repeated sacrifice of what Hebrews says was offered once; and it directs worship to the consecrated element.

The principle to recover is the memorial and covenantal character of the Supper and the reception of Christ by faith. Paul gives the cup in the same terms: “This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:25). Matthew records the institution with the bread still in His hands, “Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples” (Mat 26:26). And Luke preserves the command that defines the rite: “This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19).

pos: n. (cathedral city of Sussex; a see that changed hands with every change of crown between 1543 and 1570)
etymology: From Old English Cissanceaster, the fort of Cissa, on the Roman Noviomagus; ceaster, a walled town.
biblical_def: Chichester shows what the English Reformation looked like from a provincial see. George Day was made bishop in 1543, was deprived under Edward VI in 1551 for refusing to replace the stone altars with tables, was restored by Mary in 1553 and died in office in 1556; John Scory, an Edwardian who had fled abroad under Mary and conformed briefly on his return, was translated to Hereford; William Barlow, who had already changed his position more than once under Henry, held the see from 1559. Within twenty-seven years the diocese had four bishops of three different convictions, and its clergy and people were required to follow each. The dictionary records the see because such a sequence produces the condition Paul names and warns against: men “tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to deprive as to divest of office or dignity; to waver as to fluctuate in opinion, to be undetermined; and stedfastness as firmness, fixedness in principle.
webster_full: DEPRIVE, v.t. [L. deprivo.] To take from; to divest of office or dignity; to depose; to divest of an ecclesiastical preferment.
WAVER, v.i. To play or move to and fro; to fluctuate in opinion; to be undetermined; to be unsettled.
STEDFASTNESS, n. Firmness; fixedness in place or principle; constancy; resolution.
SLEIGHT, n. An artful trick; sly artifice; dexterous practice; cunning.
scriptures: Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
Jam 1:6
But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.
Heb 13:9
Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace; not with meats, which have not profited them that have been occupied therein.
Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know these things before, beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness.
corruption_summary: Four bishops of three convictions in twenty-seven years, as the Sussex see changed hands with Henry, Edward, Mary and Elizabeth.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the one the Tudor settlement made almost unavoidable: the belief that the doctrine of a diocese is whatever the current sovereign requires, and the career clergy that belief produces. William Barlow held four English sees under three monarchs and signed for each of them. The dictionary does not treat every conforming minister as a hypocrite, since some genuinely changed their minds and some judged that staying served their people better than leaving; but a church in which the ordinary way to keep a bishopric is to change doctrine twice has a problem the change of sovereign did not cause.

The principle to recover is stability of doctrine and the settling of the heart by grace rather than by authority. James describes the unstable man as “a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (Jam 1:6). Hebrews gives both the warning and the remedy: “Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace” (Heb 13:9). And Peter warns those who have been forewarned, to “beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness” (2Pe 3:17).

pos: n. (cathedral city of Staffordshire; see of Thomas Bentham, who had pastored the secret London congregation under Mary)
etymology: From Old English Lyccidfeld, the open land by Letocetum; later read as the field of corpses.
biblical_def: Lichfield received as its bishop in 1560 a man whose previous charge had met in private houses at night. Thomas Bentham, a Magdalen fellow expelled for his religion, spent the Marian years partly in exile at Zurich and Basle and partly in London, where from 1558 he pastored the secret Protestant congregation of the city: a gathered church of perhaps two hundred, meeting in houses and on ships, with its own discipline and its own collections for the imprisoned, which he served at the risk of burning. Under Elizabeth he was given Lichfield and Coventry, a poor and backward diocese which he worked hard and left better. The dictionary records the see because the London congregation is the plainest English example of what the New Testament usually means by a church: a company in a house. Paul greets such a company by name: “greet the church that is in their house” (Rom 16:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a congregation as an assembly met for the worship of God; to gather as to collect, to bring into one place; and secret as concealed, hidden, not seen.
webster_full: CONGREGATION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God, and for religious instruction.
GATHER, v.t. To bring together; to collect a number of separate things; to assemble.
SECRET, adj. [L. secretus.] Properly, separate; hence, concealed; hid; not revealed; private; unseen.
CONVENTICLE, n. [L. conventiculum.] An assembly or meeting; usually, a meeting of dissenters from the established church.
scriptures: Rom 16:5
Likewise greet the church that is in their house. Salute my wellbeloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ.
And when he had considered the thing, he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying.
Phm 1:2
And to our beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier, and to the church in thy house:
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
corruption_summary: Thomas Bentham's see from 1560; under Mary he had pastored the secret Protestant congregation of London at the risk of burning.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error nearer at hand runs in two directions. One is the assumption that a church is not a church without a building, a settled endowment and a recognised standing, which would have unchurched the London congregation and most of the apostolic ones. The other is the modern preference for the informal house meeting as such, detached from ordained ministry, discipline and the sacraments; Bentham's congregation had all three and was a church for that reason, not because it met in a parlour.

The principle to recover is that the church is the gathered company with Christ in the midst of it, whatever the premises. Luke shows the Jerusalem church in session in a private house while its chief apostle is in prison, “where many were gathered together praying” (Act 12:12). Paul addresses a letter to a household and to the congregation in it, “and to the church in thy house” (Phm 1:2). And Christ gives the promise that makes the smallest such meeting a church: “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20).
roots_summary: Greek ekklesia (G1577), a church or assembly; Greek sunago (G4863), to gather together.
roots_lines: Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly, those called out, a church; Romans 16:5.
Greek sunago (G4863) — to lead together, to assemble; Matthew 18:20.
Greek oikos (G3624) — a house, a household; Philemon 1:2.
Greek proseuchomai (G4336) — to pray; Acts 12:12.
Greek aparche (G536) — firstfruits, the first portion; Romans 16:5.
usage: “greet the church that is in their house” (Rom 16:5) — the secret London congregation, pastored from 1558.
“where many were gathered together praying” (Act 12:12) — meetings in houses and on ships, with its own discipline.
“For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20) — given Lichfield and Coventry in 1560.

pos: n. (cathedral city of the English border; see of Owen Oglethorpe, who crowned Elizabeth I and then refused her supremacy)
etymology: From Brittonic Caer Luel, the fort of Luguvalium; caer, a fortified place.
biblical_def: Carlisle guards the western end of the Scottish border and its bishop in 1559 did the English church an awkward service. Owen Oglethorpe, a Marian appointee, was the only bishop willing to crown Elizabeth I when the archbishopric of Canterbury was vacant and the rest of the bench, foreseeing what her reign would mean, declined; he performed the coronation on 15 January 1559, though he would not omit the elevation of the host and she walked out of that part of the mass. Within months he refused the Oath of Supremacy, was deprived of his see, and died before the year was out. The dictionary records him because he distinguished exactly between two obediences, rendering the civil honour and withholding what he believed belonged to God. “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines supremacy as the highest authority or power; an oath as a solemn affirmation with an appeal to God; and to render as to give in return, to pay back what is due.
webster_full: SUPREMACY, n. State of being supreme or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
RENDER, v.t. [L. reddo.] To return; to pay back; to give in return; to give what is due.
CORONATION, n. The act or solemnity of crowning a king or other sovereign.
scriptures: They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
Dan 6:10

Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.
Dan 3:12

There are certain Jews whom thou hast set over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
corruption_summary: Owen Oglethorpe crowned Elizabeth I in January 1559 when the other bishops refused, then lost the see for refusing her supremacy.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions meet here and the dictionary names both, since Oglethorpe was wrong on one count and right on the other. He was wrong in the doctrine he was defending, the Roman mass with the elevation of the host, which the Reformation rejected on the grounds set out at Rochester. He was right in refusing a royal supremacy over the church of Christ, which the Tudor settlement asserted and which the dictionary rejects as firmly in a Protestant prince as in a pope; the headship of the church is not in the gift of a parliament.

The principle to recover is the division of obediences, with honour rendered to the ruler and conscience reserved to God. Daniel went on praying at his open window when the writing was signed, “as he did aforetime” (Dan 6:10), neither hiding nor rebelling. The accusation against the three in Babylon was precisely this limited refusal: “they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:12). And Peter sets all four duties in one line without letting any swallow another: “Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king” (1Pe 2:17).
roots_summary: Greek apodidomi (G591), to render; Greek timao (G5091), to honour.
roots_lines: Greek apodidomi (G591) — to give back, to render what is due; Matthew 22:21.
Greek timao (G5091) — to honour, to value, to esteem; 1 Peter 2:17.
Greek phobeo (G5399) — to fear, to reverence; 1 Peter 2:17.
Hebrew bera (H1289) — to kneel, to bless; Daniel 6:10.
Hebrew pelach (H6399) — to serve, to worship, to minister; Daniel 3:12.
usage: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21) — the coronation of 15 January 1559.
“as he did aforetime” (Dan 6:10) — he would not omit the elevation of the host.
“Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king” (1Pe 2:17) — deprived for refusing the Oath of Supremacy and dead within the year.

pos: n. (cathedral city of the Cambridgeshire fens; see of Richard Cox, who fought John Knox over the Prayer Book at Frankfurt)
etymology: From Old English Elig, the island of eels; ēl, an eel, and īg, an island.
biblical_def: Ely sits on a low island in the fens and had for its Elizabethan bishop a man whose name belongs to one of the Reformation's least edifying quarrels. Richard Cox had been tutor to Edward VI and a principal hand in the Edwardian Prayer Book, and in 1554 he arrived among the English exiles at Frankfurt, where the congregation under John Knox and others had agreed a simpler order of service. Cox insisted on the English book entire, worked to exclude Knox from the city by representing his writings against the Emperor to the magistrates, and carried the point; Knox withdrew to Geneva. Cox became bishop of Ely in 1559 and held it twenty-one years. The dictionary records the see because the Frankfurt troubles are the exiles' own indictment, and the apostle's diagnosis of such a quarrel is unsparing: “Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory” (Php 2:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines strife as exertion or contention for superiority, contest; vainglory as empty pride, pride above desert; and carnal as fleshly, not spiritual.
webster_full: STRIFE, n. Exertion or contention for superiority; contest of emulation, either by intellectual or physical efforts; discord; contention.
VAINGLORY, n. Vanity; empty pride; undue elation of mind; pride above desert or without merit.
CARNAL, adj. [L. carnalis.] Fleshly; pertaining to flesh; not spiritual; opposed to spiritual.
LOWLINESS, n. Humility; freedom from pride; meanness of condition.
scriptures: Php 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
Php 2:4
Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men?
Gal 5:15
But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.
corruption_summary: Richard Cox's see from 1559; at Frankfurt in 1554 he forced the English Prayer Book on the exiles and had Knox excluded from the city.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of the civil magistrate to settle a dispute among brethren, which is what Cox did at Frankfurt when he laid Knox's book before the city council. Both parties had a case about the Prayer Book, and the dictionary is on the simpler side of that argument; but the method was indefensible, and it was used by men who were in Frankfurt because magistrates at home had done the same thing to them. The matching failure was the exiles' refusal to settle the matter among themselves while they had the opportunity, which carried the quarrel home and into the next century.

The principle to recover is that brethren in dispute are to prefer one another and to watch what contention does to a church. Paul adds the practical test: “Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others” (Php 2:4). He calls the Corinthian factions by their right name, since “whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal” (1Co 3:3). And he warns the Galatians where it ends: “if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another” (Gal 5:15).

roots_lines: Greek eritheia (G2052) — contention, faction, party spirit; Philippians 2:3.
Greek kenodoxia (G2754) — empty glory, vainglory, conceit; Philippians 2:3.
Greek tapeinophrosune (G5012) — lowliness of mind, humility; Philippians 2:3.
Greek sarkikos (G4559) — carnal, fleshly; 1 Corinthians 3:3.
Greek analisko (G355) — to consume, to use up, to destroy; Galatians 5:15.

“whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal” (1Co 3:3) — Knox withdrew to Geneva.
“if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another” (Gal 5:15) — Cox held Ely twenty-one years.

pos: n. (cathedral city of Northamptonshire; a see created in 1541 out of a dissolved abbey)
etymology: From Old English, the borough of St Peter; earlier Medeshamstede, the homestead by the whirlpool.
biblical_def: Peterborough is one of six English cathedrals that exist because a monastery was dissolved. The Benedictine abbey of Medeshamstede, refounded after the Danes burnt it, surrendered to the crown in 1539; two years later Henry VIII made its church the cathedral of a new diocese carved out of Lincoln, with the last abbot as the first bishop and much of the monastic endowment retained for the chapter and a school. Catherine of Aragon had been buried there in 1536, and Mary Queen of Scots was buried there in 1587 before her removal to Westminster. The dictionary records the see because it is the one good use the dissolution was put to, and because the question it raises about spoil is a real one. Haggai's promise about a poorer second house is the right text: “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts” (Hag 2:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dissolution as the act of breaking up an assembly or institution; an endowment as the act of settling a fund for the support of an institution; and to repair as to restore after decay.
webster_full: DISSOLUTION, n. [L. dissolutio.] The act of breaking up an assembly, or of putting an end to a corporation or institution.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of a public institution.
REPAIR, v.t. [L. reparo.] To restore to a sound state after decay or injury; to rebuild a part decayed or lost.
SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; plunder; pillage; booty.
scriptures: Hag 2:9
The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts: and in this place will I give peace, saith the LORD of hosts.
Isa 61:4
And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.
Zec 1:16
Therefore thus saith the LORD; I am returned to Jerusalem with mercies: my house shall be built in it, saith the LORD of hosts, and a line shall be stretched forth upon Jerusalem.
Heb 3:4
For every house is builded by some man; but he that built all things is God.
corruption_summary: A see created in 1541 from the dissolved abbey of Medeshamstede, with the last abbot as its first bishop and the endowment kept for a chapter and school.
corruption_paragraphs: Two things are to be named and they do not cancel each other. The monastic system the dissolution ended was a genuine corruption: a vowed life presented as a higher calling, a treasury of merit, masses said for the dead, and in England by 1530 a great deal of idleness on a very large endowment. The dissolution itself was also a corruption, carried out for the crown's revenue, with libraries destroyed, hospitals and almshouses closed along with the abbeys, and the greater part of the land sold to courtiers. Peterborough is noteworthy because at six sites the money was actually turned to preaching and teaching.

The principle to recover is that God builds, repairs and uses what men have ruined, and that He gets the credit when the second house is poorer than the first. Isaiah promises that they shall “build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations” (Isa 61:4). Zechariah has the Lord return with the measuring line: “my house shall be built in it, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 1:16). And Hebrews puts every builder in his place: “For every house is builded by some man; but he that built all things is God” (Heb 3:4).
roots_summary: Hebrew kabod (H3519), glory; Hebrew chorbah (H2723), a waste place.
roots_lines: Hebrew kabod (H3519) — weight, honour, glory; Haggai 2:9.
Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a waste, a desolation, a ruin; Isaiah 61:4.
Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, welfare, completeness; Haggai 2:9.
Hebrew qav (H6957) — a measuring line, a cord; Zechariah 1:16.
Greek kataskeuazo (G2680) — to prepare, to build, to furnish; Hebrews 3:4.
usage: “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts” (Hag 2:9) — the abbey surrendered in 1539, the see created in 1541.
“build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations” (Isa 61:4) — the endowment kept for a chapter and a school.
“For every house is builded by some man; but he that built all things is God” (Heb 3:4) — Catherine of Aragon buried here in 1536.
